prompt:
You are analysing one document co-written by the AI-safety researcher Owain Evans, to find what DISTINGUISHES his research taste from the rest of the field. Output ONLY a JSON object, no prose, no code fences.

Document: "AMA on Truthful AI: Owen Cotton-Barratt, Owain Evans & co-authors" (2021-10-22); kind=post; his author position=solo. For solo, first- or last-author work the choices are plausibly his; for middle-author work, mark attribution "team".

What we already know and do NOT want: he shares the field's consensus. Careful controls, matched baselines, hedged claims, replication, error bars, realistic setups, reporting rates, avoiding overclaiming, caring about safety. A blind judge already predicts all of that. Items of that kind are useless here, however well quoted.

What we want: his DEPARTURES. Places where this work makes a choice that a typical strong ML-safety researcher in 2021, facing the same problem with the same resources, would probably have made differently. The default you name must be a reasonable, defensible choice that competent researchers actually make (for example: study a capability with interpretability rather than behaviour; use the largest frontier model; build a broad benchmark; fine-tune only when prompting fails; frame the work around a threat model; avoid speculative or "weird" phenomena), never a strawman or a mistake.

Part A, "contrasts" (0-6 items; return fewer rather than include consensus items):
  dpoint: "Q" (which question or phenomenon to study at all), "D1" (experiment design), "D2" (which data, models, measurements), "D3" (accept or reject a result), "D4" (pursue or abandon a line), "D5" (how to read a surprising result), "D6" (what to claim, how to present it)
  default: one sentence, what a typical strong ML-safety researcher would do here instead
  choice: one sentence, what this work did
  why: the reason the document gives, or ""
  quote: a VERBATIM passage of 15-60 words, copied character-for-character from the document, that shows the choice. Do not paraphrase, stitch or fix typos.
  distinct: 1-3 (3 = most strong researchers would have taken the default)
  attribution: "own" or "team"

Part B, "axes": for each of these trade-off axes on which the document gives real evidence (skip the rest; most documents touch 0-4 of them), the pole the work leans to:
  - construct-scope: 1 = A narrow operational definition that isolates one sub-component of the behaviour. | 2 = A broad definition that covers the behaviour as it shows up in practice.
  - purpose: 1 = Informing a concrete decision someone has to make, such as whether a model is safe to deploy. | 2 = Understanding the phenomenon better, even if no decision depends on the result yet.
  - control-vs-realism: 1 = A controlled setup where one variable changes and the cause of any difference is clear. | 2 = A realistic setup with many natural cues at once, closer to what the model meets in deployment.
  - scale-vs-craft: 1 = Many variants, generated with a model and checked in bulk. | 2 = A few variants, each written and checked by hand.
  - elicitation: 1 = Maximum effort: the best prompt, scaffold and tools you can find. | 2 = Default behaviour: the model as users actually run it.
  - grading: 1 = An LLM judge over many transcripts. | 2 = Human or rule-based grading over fewer transcripts.
  - awareness-signal: 1 = Asking the model directly, after the episode, whether it thinks it was an evaluation. | 2 = Inferring it from the model's behaviour and reasoning during the episode, without asking.
  - items-vs-samples: 1 = More distinct items, one or two samples each. | 2 = Fewer items, many samples each, so you can tell an item that never trips the model from one that sometimes does.
  - evidence-bar: 1 = Re-test it on fresh samples before deciding. | 2 = Drop it and spend the budget on the next idea.
  - breadth-vs-depth: 1 = Move to a different direction. | 2 = Stay with it to find out why the results are mixed.
  - reading: 1 = Read a batch of transcripts closely. | 2 = Break the aggregate numbers down by condition and item.
  - explanation-prior: 1 = Look for a setup artefact before trusting it. | 2 = Run a direct follow-up that would confirm the effect, which also exposes most artefacts.
  - claim-scope: 1 = A narrow claim, limited to the exact setup you tested. | 2 = A general claim about the behaviour, stated with its uncertainty.
  - openness: 1 = Keep the items private, so future models can't train on them. | 2 = Publish the items, so others can reproduce and build on the results.
  item form: {"axis": "<name>", "pole": 1 or 2, "strength": 1-3, "quote": "<verbatim 15-60 words>"}

Part C, "new_axes" (0-3): other dimensions on which ML-safety researchers genuinely split and on which this work takes a clear side, such as how questions get chosen, empirical vs conceptual framing, preferred experimental paradigm, black-box vs white-box methods, model scale, toy vs realistic tasks, speed vs polish of release.
  item form: {"name": "<short>", "pole_a": "<one side>", "pole_b": "<other side>", "his_pole": "a" or "b", "quote": "<verbatim 15-60 words>"}

Return {"doc_summary": "<=2 sentences", "contrasts": [...], "axes": [...], "new_axes": [...]}

We just published a long [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.06674) on Truthful AI ([overview post](/api/post/aBixCPqSnTsPsTJBQ)). We’ll be running an Ask Me Anything on truthful AI from Tuesday (October 26) to Wednesday (October 27) at this post. 
 
You may wish to ask about:

1. Anything discussed in the Truthful AI paper (e.g. concepts, costs/benefits, governance, development, connections to beneficial AI).
2. Truthfulness for current language models (e.g. [TruthfulQA](/api/post/PF58wEdztZFX2dSue) — which [Owain](/api/user/owain_evans) co-authored)
3. Promising research directions on truthful AI
4. Anything else (unrelated to truthful AI) — although we are more likely to answer questions about truthful AI.

If you want to ask something just post a top-level comment. Also feel free to make comments that are not questions (e.g. objections or suggestions).
